answer.rationale: The strongest available signal is temporal: a release landed 2h ago and write-path p99 began climbing ~90m ago, which fits a post-deploy regression better than pure load (settlement peaks are recurring and memory_b3 says headroom historically absorbed surge, so capacity is less likely the binding constraint). Regional failover (memory_b2) would move a bad build with the traffic and is the wrong tool for a code-induced regression; read-replica routing (memory_b5) relieves read pressure on the primary but this is a write-path problem; circuit breakers (memory_b4) fit a failing external dependency, and there is no partner-outage signal here. So rollback is the best-supported single intervention. I want memory_b1 verified above all because it is the only inherited record that directly underwrites 'rollback is safe and effective,' and my whole plan rests on it. Its summary claims the rollback 'finished without customer impact,' but the day-18 conditions are unknown to me from the summary alone: if that rollback ran during a quiet window rather than at settlement peak with heavy writes, its reassurance does not transfer, and a schema or data-format migration in the current release could make a reverse-deploy lossy for in-flight writes -- exactly the failure the primary objective forbids. That is the downstream risk I am flagging. I explicitly do not treat the release-to-latency correlation as established causation; an unrelated slow resource leak or a peak-specific contention cliff remain live alternatives. Accordingly I stage the rollback rather than fire it globally, borrowing the canary discipline from memory_b6: revert on a small guarded slice of write-path capacity, drain in-flight writes before cutting over, and watch p99 and write-loss counters on that slice. If p99 recovers on the reverted cohort and not elsewhere, causation is confirmed and I widen in the next window; if it does not, I have spent little, preserved customer writes, and cleared rollback from the hypothesis set so the next window can test load or dependency causes instead. If archive review shows the day-18 rollback was a low-traffic, no-migration case, I will treat its safety claim as non-transferable and tighten the guard further before touching the peak path.
